courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Memory cost, ablations, failure modes and gsplat in practice
md: 3DGS trades memory for speed: hundreds of megabytes of explicit parameters instead of a few megabytes of network weights, in exchange for rendering at well over 30 FPS and training in tens of minutes.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Add-one-in vs leave-one-out on a fixed harness
md: Removing a stage is not always a clean subtraction. You must decide what replaces it: no rewrite at all, or a trivial rewrite; BM25 alone, or BM25 with more candidates to keep the reranker's input size equal. State the replacement, because different choices give different deltas.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: IDOR and BOLA: changing one number in the URL
md: The OWASP API Security Top 10 warns that comparing the session's user id with an id parameter covers only a small subset of BOLA cases. Objects are often shared (a team folder, a manager viewing a report), so the real question is "may this user perform this action on this object under our policy", which lessons 11 and 12 turn into one reusable check.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Enforce authorization in one place: deny by default, policy engines
md: Central does not mean single. Next.js apps that checked access only in middleware were exposed when CVE-2025-29927 let requests skip middleware (lesson 7). Decide policy in one place, but enforce it at more than one layer: at the route, and again at the data (scoped queries, RLS).

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Kerberoasting: service tickets that can be cracked offline
md: Moving a service account to AES is not a fix by itself. An AES ticket for `Summer2019!` is still crackable; it only costs more per guess. The fix is a password nobody can guess: a gMSA or a long random secret.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: AD CS: when a certificate template hands out admin
md: In AD a certificate trusted for client authentication is a password that survives password resets. ESC1 is a template that lets any user choose the name in the certificate. Audit templates, treat CAs as Tier 0, watch 4886 and 4887 for mismatched subjects, and revoke rather than reset.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: OOXML: a zip of XML parts, and links that fetch remote content
md: A document can be dangerous with zero bytes of code inside it. In OOXML, read every .rels part: one line with TargetMode External can be the whole attack.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Anti-debugging and anti-VM: recognising checks and getting past them
md: An empty sandbox report means 'not observed in this environment', never 'benign'. Say exactly that in your notes and in any verdict you hand to the SOC.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Format string bugs as read and write primitives
md: A format string bug is a primitive factory: the read directives leak, and %n writes. The cure is structural and cheap: constant format strings, enforced by -Werror=format-security and static analysis.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: OPSEC through the defender's eyes: every action leaves a trace
md: Map each emulated step to the log that must record it before the exercise. If the step passes unseen, the gap is in one of three places: the data was never collected, it was collected but no rule looked, or a rule fired and nobody acted. Lesson 12 names these gaps.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: An agent benchmark is a task, an environment and a grader
md: Outcome grading is not the same as correct behavior. A grader only sees what it checks: tests that cover one interpretation, a database diff, an answer string. Anything outside the check (rudeness, a policy step skipped, an unrelated file deleted) can pass silently.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Keeping the context window under control
md: Compaction is lossy. The Agent SDK docs warn that specific instructions from early in the conversation may not survive a summary. Put durable rules in a file that is re-injected on every request (the SDK uses CLAUDE.md for this), not only in the first user message.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Evaluating memory and the ways it fails
md: Memory is untrusted input that outlives the session. Record provenance on every write (user said it, a tool returned it, the model inferred it), only promote user-stated facts to instructions-like status, show retrieved memories to the model as quoted data, and give users a way to view and delete what the agent remembers.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Reward design: hidden tests, partial credit and judges
md: Partial credit is not automatically better. A reward that counts tests which already passed pays the agent for the starting state, so on hard tasks the policy can learn that touching nothing beats trying. Credit only the change you want, and make breaking existing behavior cost something.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: EchoLeak: one email, zero clicks, Copilot leaks
md: Every one of Microsoft's controls existed and every one had a gap. Layered defence only works if each layer is complete on its own: all Markdown syntaxes, all allowlisted domains, all retrieval paths.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Misinformation and unbounded consumption
md: Agents multiply consumption: one user request can trigger many model calls and tool calls in a loop. Cap steps per task and total tokens per task, not only per request, or a confused agent (or an injected one) can run until the budget is gone.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Generating crystals with diffusion: CDVAE to MatterGen
md: A generator's novelty number is only as good as its reference set and structure matcher. Note that the same disorder issue from the GNoME critique appears here: the synthesized TaCr2O6 was disordered, and MatterGen's ordered-disordered matcher exists so that an ordered variant of a known disordered compound is not counted as new.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Distortion-free sampling: the Gumbel trick and SynthID tournaments
md: Green lists shift probabilities toward a keyed subset (distortionary). Gumbel sampling and two-competitor tournaments keep each token's distribution exact and hide the signal in correlations between chosen tokens and keyed random values. All of them need entropy to work.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Replaying workloads to compare allocators
md: Workflow: capture once with an interposer, analyze with a heap profiler to find what to fix in code, convert to a workload, then replay that one workload against each allocator or tuning and compare RSS against ideal RSS.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Anomalies in time: seasonal baselines and robust residuals
md: For time series, first remove what is predictable (seasonality and level), then apply a robust score to the residual. The detector is only as good as the baseline: a residual is anomalous relative to a model of normal for that moment.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: OAuth 2.0: delegated access without sharing a password
md: OAuth is about **authorization**: letting a client act on a user's behalf with limited scope. The access token is meant for the resource server, not for the client to learn who the user is. Logging users in needs OpenID Connect (lesson 10).

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Validating a JWT correctly: algorithm, signature, iss, aud, exp, nbf
md: Misconception: "we validate the token at the API gateway, so services can just decode it." Then any path around the gateway, and any token for another audience the gateway also accepts, reaches services that trust it blindly. Each service should at least check the audience meant for it.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: What an application security programme is, and who owns what
md: "Security owns security" is the most common misconception. A central team that tries to fix everything becomes a bottleneck and then gets bypassed. The working model: developers own fixes, the security team owns the system that makes fixes happen.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Testing the running app: DAST, IAST, SCA recall and fuzzing in CI
md: No method sees everything. SAST and SCA see code and dependencies early; DAST sees the deployed surface; IAST sees runtime paths the tests exercise; fuzzing sees parsers under abuse. Pick by what your application does: an API with a heavy parser needs fuzzing more than a static brochure site does.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Metrics that matter: time to remediate, open age and coverage
md: Measure what is still open and what you cannot see. Mean time to remediate, open age, SLA compliance and coverage together describe a programme; any one alone can be gamed by accident.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Why a question is not a short version of its answer
md: Misconception: *a text's embedding is a fixed property of the text.* In a role-aware model the same string gets one vector as a query and a different vector as a document, by design. Which vector you get depends on how you called the model.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Rate limits as token buckets: RPM, token limits and headers
md: Do not cache or replay a 429 as if it were an answer. RFC 6585 says responses with status 429 "MUST NOT be stored by a cache". Also note that a 429 is not always temporary: Anthropic returns 429 without a `retry-after` header when an organization reaches its monthly spend cap, and retrying keeps failing until access resumes.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Why counter++ from two threads loses updates
md: `volatile` does not fix this. In C and C++ it stops the compiler from removing or reordering accesses within one thread, which suits signal handlers and memory-mapped I/O, but cppreference states it is not suitable for communication between threads. A volatile `counter++` is still a separate read and write.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Sigmoid outputs and pooling patch scores into a clip score
md: Mean pooling suits sounds that last (rain, engine hum, music) and resists one-patch glitches. Max pooling catches short events (a bark, a door slam, a gunshot) but turns any single false patch into a clip-level false alarm. PANNs combines both inside the network: its global pooling sums the time-averaged and the time-maximized feature vectors.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Slow on purpose: bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2id and cost parameters
md: Store passwords with Argon2id (or scrypt, or bcrypt for legacy), a unique salt per user, and a cost tuned as high as your login traffic allows. Record the parameters with each hash, and raise them over time.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Passkeys and WebAuthn: why phishing stops working
md: Passkeys resist phishing because the browser binds every signature to the real site's origin and the credential to the site's domain. The user's judgment is not part of the security argument.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: One API in front of many models: the Converse call
md: Converse unifies the **shape** of requests and responses, not the **behavior** of models. Models still differ in quality, context length, supported content types and tool support, which the docs list per model. A one-line modelId swap is easy; validating that the new model is good enough is still your job.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Rust binaries: mangled paths, slices and panics
md: In Rust binaries, follow the panics. Every `panic_bounds_check`, `unwrap` failure and `expect` message carries a source location or message string. Even when symbols are stripped, cross-references to those strings map functions back to files and lines in the original crate.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Training from scratch: latent weights and the STE
md: Training a BitNet is not cheaper than training an FP16 model with today's code. Latent weights, gradients and optimizer states are high precision, and the FAQ notes their training ran in FP16/BF16 with no speedup. The savings are at inference.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Branchless code: cmov, masks and lookup tables
md: Branchless code trades a *possible* misprediction for *always* doing the work of both sides plus the select. Always check the compiler output (Compiler Explorer, the godbolt.org website that shows the assembly a compiler produces, or the `-S` flag, which makes the compiler write assembly instead of an object file) before hand-rewriting: the optimizer may already have done it, or may have a good reason not to.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Choosing an engine: tradeoffs, write stalls and failure modes
md: Misconception: "LSM-trees have no write amplification because they only write sequentially." They write sequentially, but every byte is rewritten as it moves down levels: about 33x in RocksDB's leveled example. The win is in I/O pattern and batching, not in writing less, and on some workloads a B+tree writes fewer bytes.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Resilience, continuity and recovery: the words and the plans
md: Resilience is the outcome; continuity is about business processes; contingency and disaster recovery are about systems and sites. A real organisation needs a small family of plans that agree with each other on who decides, in what order things come back, and who speaks.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Backups nobody restored: monitoring and testing that prove recovery
md: Every backup needs an owner, a check on every step, an alert on missing success through a separate channel, and an automated restore test that measures time and verifies content. Rehearsed restores (Gmail 2011) produce estimates; unrehearsed ones (GitLab 2017) produce surprises.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: When recovery tools fail too: CrowdStrike 2024, keys and break-glass
md: Draw the dependency graph of recovery itself and look for cycles. Break them with out-of-band copies (exported keys, printed runbooks, separate comms), break-glass accounts that depend on nothing in the estate, and tested access paths for every security tool you will need on the worst day.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Patches: run the big model once per group of bytes
md: A patch is a group of bytes that the big model treats as one position, with no fixed vocabulary. Average patch size sets the compute: forward cost per byte is about $2(m_g/P + m_\ell)$.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Learning where to cut: from character models to H-Net
md: The design space for byte models is who decides the cut: a fixed rate, a hand-written rule, a separate model (BLT), or the model's own loss (H-Net's cosine router plus a ratio loss). Learned cuts remove BLT's separately trained entropy model, at the cost of new machinery to make a discrete choice trainable.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Safe wrappers over unsafe code: split_at_mut and soundness
md: A clean Miri run is evidence, not proof. Miri is dynamic: it only checks the paths your tests execute, and the Book notes it does not cover every way code can be unsound. Combine it with tests that hit the edge cases, such as mid = len and mid = len + 1.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Where a line may live: sets, ways and tags
md: Power-of-two strides are a trap. In this L1d every address 4096 bytes apart maps to the same set, and a set has only 8 ways. Walking a column of `double m[N][512]` (rows of exactly 4 KB) puts every line in one set: only 8 of them can be cached at once even though the cache holds 512 lines.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: The local replacement model makes every edge linear
md: Matching the real model's outputs exactly on prompt $p$ does not mean the local replacement model uses the same mechanism. The paper compares it to a Taylor approximation: it agrees at the point and drifts as you move away, which is why interventions are needed later.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Why raw clicks teach a ranker to repeat itself
md: Under position bias, $P(\text{click}) = P(\text{examined at rank } k) \times P(\text{click} \mid \text{examined})$. Clicks are biased labels because the first factor depends on the old ranking, not on the document.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: DOM-based XSS: when the bug lives in your JavaScript
md: The URL fragment (everything after `#`) is never sent to the server, as MDN's URL guide notes. A DOM XSS that reads `location.hash` leaves no trace in access logs and is invisible to a WAF. It has to be found in the JavaScript itself, by code review, by tests, or by browser-side tools such as DOM Invader, a tool preinstalled as an extension in Burp Suite's built-in browser that tracks sources reaching sinks.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: The contrastive loss on a 4 x 4 batch
md: A common misreading: the off-diagonal pairs are not known to be unrelated. Two captions in a batch may both describe dogs. The loss still pushes them apart, so duplicates and near-duplicates in a batch become false negatives. With 32,768 pairs per batch this is noise the model tolerates, not something the loss detects.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Azure and Google Cloud: activity, resource and audit logs
md: Misconception: "the activity log shows who read the secret". It shows who changed the vault's access policy. Reading a secret is a data plane operation that appears only in Key Vault resource logs, and only if a diagnostic setting was sending them before the read.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Containing without breaking production, and a cloud IR runbook
md: Contain in one coordinated window: close the source, revoke sessions and keys, cut the destination if needed, with production owners ready for the blip. Revocation without closing the source lets the attacker fetch fresh credentials; closing the source without revocation leaves stolen ones working.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Human access: LastPass 2022, Identity Center and break-glass
md: "We have MFA, so stolen passwords do not matter" is the misconception LastPass disproves. MFA protects the sign-in it guards. Long-lived access keys, keys stored in notes and anything readable from an already compromised device are outside its reach. Remove standing credentials, require phishing-resistant MFA, and treat engineer endpoints as part of production.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Least privilege, wildcards and the Capital One role
md: `"Resource": "*"` is not always a mistake (a few actions, such as `s3:ListAllMyBuckets`, have no narrower resource), but `"Action": "*"` or `"service:*"` on `"Resource": "*"` in an application's role almost always is. Treat each one as a finding that needs a written reason.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: What k-means actually optimises
md: Inertia is the *entire* definition of a good clustering in k-means. Anything you believe about your clusters that inertia does not measure, such as "this point is an outlier" or "this group is a long thin chain", k-means cannot express.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: End to end: grouping a million log lines into named failure patterns
md: Cluster names come from word statistics, not from causes. Two messages from different systems that share a phrase will land together, and one rare but critical message can hide inside a big cluster. Always read a few members of every cluster, and treat the HDBSCAN noise set as a queue to review, not a bin to discard.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Inside a vectorized pipeline: primitives and selection vectors
md: Vectorized engines split work into type-specialized primitives over arrays, and pass filters along as lists of positions instead of moving data.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Why code breaks at -O2: undefined behavior as an optimization license
md: Misconception: "it works at -O0, so -O2 has a compiler bug." Compiler bugs exist, but UB in the program is far more common. And -O0 is no safe harbor: GCC folds `a + b < a` to `b < 0` even at -O0, and the next compiler version may exploit UB that this one ignores.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Measure it: benchmarking builds and an end-to-end tuning run
md: Measure time with repetitions, medians and spreads, on representative input, one change at a time. Explain each gain with counters and compiler remarks. On this program LTO gave the big win, PGO a few percent, and -O3 and -mcpu=native nothing measurable.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Why a concurrent test can pass a million times and still be wrong
md: A concurrent test that passes tells you only that the schedules your machine happened to pick were fine. To learn anything about the others you must either enumerate schedules (loom) or check the ordering rules on the schedule you got (TSan).

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: Self-consistency: every point on a trajectory maps to its origin
md: A consistency model is not a one-step denoiser. A network trained with plain squared-error regression (the L2 loss) to $x_0$ from $x_T$ learns the conditional mean, which is blurry for images and collapses in the toy. The consistency function is a deterministic map along ODE trajectories, so its outputs keep the full data spread.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Why hash mod N reshuffles almost every key
md: A central lookup table (key range to server) also gives minimal movement, and many databases use one. The catch is that every client must fetch and agree on the table. Consistent hashing lets each client compute the owner from the key and the server list alone.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Too few results: relaxation ladders and post-hoc constraints
md: Three layers, three tools: per-document requirements are **filters**, per-document preferences are a **weighted score**, and requirements on the list as a whole are a **re-ranking pass**. When filters starve the list, relax in a declared order, keep the non-negotiables hard, and say what you relaxed.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: One kernel, many tenants: the container threat model
md: Misconception: "root in a container is harmless because it is only container root". Without user namespaces, UID 0 inside the container is UID 0 on the host, held back only by dropped capabilities, seccomp and the LSM. Remove those fences, or find a bug in them, and it is real root.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: A hardened pod spec, line by line
md: Hardened default for application pods: no token, non-root, RuntimeDefault seccomp, no privilege escalation, read-only root filesystem, drop ALL capabilities, explicit writable volumes, resource limits, image by digest.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Network policies: from default allow to default deny
md: Misconception: "the database is internal, so it is not exposed". Internal means reachable by every pod in the cluster unless a policy says otherwise. Treat the pod network as a hostile network.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a hardening map and where to practise
md: Legal line: everything in this course is for clusters you own or have written permission to test. Scanning the internet for open kubelets or Docker APIs, or using one you find, is unauthorised access under laws such as the US CFAA and the UK Computer Misuse Act, whatever the intent.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: A five-turn session: diffs, state and generated queries
md: Let the LLM decide **what changed**; let code decide **what the state is** and **what the query is**. This split makes carryover free, makes every change visible in logs, and turns the hardest part into a small, testable classification problem.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Poking the chain: truncate it, break it, reword it
md: Each test rules out one failure class, nothing more. A CoT that passes truncation and mistake tests is causally used, but it can still omit a factor (as in Turpin's hints). Lanham et al. call this a defense-in-depth approach: no single test certifies faithfulness.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Building and scoring a CoT monitor
md: Set the threshold from a false-positive budget on clean runs, report recall at that FPR, and expect low precision when misbehavior is rare. Score CoT and actions separately and combine them: the CoT catches subtle intent, the actions keep a persuasive CoT from talking the monitor out of an obvious flag.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
md: A cross-encoder is not a better embedding model. It has no vector output you could store in a vector database. If someone asks you to index a corpus with a reranker, the answer is that you cannot: the score exists only for a specific query.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: What cryptography promises, and to whom
md: Ask of every design: which of confidentiality, integrity and authenticity do I need, against whom, and where does the key live? A primitive that gives one goal never silently gives the others.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Randomness: where keys come from, and the Debian disaster
md: A random-looking output says nothing about its entropy. Debian's weak keys passed every visual check; their weakness was only visible by counting how many could exist.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Fixed IVs in homemade protocols: Zerologon
md: An IV or nonce is an input with a contract (unique, sometimes unpredictable), not a constant. When a design fixes it, ask what the mode's security proof assumes, who controls the plaintext, and how many attempts an attacker gets. Better: use a standard authenticated protocol instead of designing one.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Why a fast GEMM is a hierarchy of tiles
md: Every level of the hierarchy does the same thing: stage a tile in a faster, smaller memory and reuse it across as many math operations as the capacity of that memory allows. Tile shapes are the main tuning knobs of a CUTLASS GEMM.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: The CUTLASS 3.x API, epilogues and tuning tradeoffs
md: Fast CUTLASS kernels come from a few choices: tile shape (reuse versus occupancy and wave fit), stage count (latency hiding versus shared memory), kernel schedule (cooperative or ping-pong) and the epilogue fusion. CuTe layouts make each choice a type parameter instead of a rewrite.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
md: CXL makes memory placement a policy problem again. The hardware gives you a slower, bigger NUMA tier; the operating system (tiering) or the cluster manager (pooling) must keep hot data local and push only cold or untouched data to it.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The UK Computer Misuse Act, section by section
md: Under section 1 a failed attempt can be enough: the offence is about intent and knowledge, not success. 'I didn't get in' is not a defence to trying.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Export controls: Wassenaar and 'intrusion software'
md: "It's only code" is not an export defence. Sending exploit technology abroad can need a licence, and US rules also cover releasing controlled technology to foreign persons at home (a "deemed export", which the 2021 rule names). Disclosure to the people who will fix the bug is the carved-out case; selling capability is not.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Cover-ups and whistleblowing: Uber's CSO and Twitter's security lead
md: "Nobody asked me directly" is weak protection. Misprision is about *active concealment* of a known felony, and obstruction can be committed by causing others not to disclose. Changing records, drafting the NDA and signing statements you know mislead are acts, not silence.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Upweighting means repeating: epochs, data limits and domain weights
md: Epochs = weight x budget / unique tokens. Up to about 4 epochs repetition costs almost nothing; beyond that each pass is worth less, and by about 40 it is worthless. Cap epochs per domain and give the surplus to domains that still have unique data.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Why a loop over objects wastes most of each cache line
md: Memory moves in cache lines. Lay out data so that the bytes a hot loop needs are packed together, and the bytes it skips live somewhere else.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Classification: levels, impact and the high-water mark
md: Classify by the damage of disclosure (and of tampering or loss), not by how the data looks. Rate each information type, take the high-water mark for systems, and attach the result as a label that tools can read.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: How DLP recognises sensitive content
md: DLP is only as good as its detector's precision. Prefer labels and exact data match over generic patterns where you can; require context for high confidence; and measure precision on real traffic before turning on blocking. Hashed SSNs are not anonymous: with about a billion possible values, anyone holding the salt can hash them all, so guard the EDM hash file and salt as Restricted data.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Honeypots by interaction: low, medium and high
md: "High interaction" is not "better". It is more informative and more dangerous. Choose the lowest level that answers your question: for internal detection, a decoy that only needs to notice a login attempt does not need a real shell.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Legal, ethical and safety limits of deception
md: Before deploying a decoy, write down: who approved it, what it records, who can see that data and for how long, how it is contained, and the conditions under which it is switched off. Engage calls the last part gating criteria.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Replaying failures, the limits of DST, and who uses it
md: A passing simulation is only as good as its fault model and its oracles. If your simulated disk never loses unsynced writes, you have not tested crash recovery; if no oracle checks liveness, a stuck cluster passes.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Drift detection: when the cloud stops matching the code
md: Do not "fix" drift by blindly running apply from the drift job. The job holds a read-only role on purpose, and an automatic revert can undo an emergency change in the middle of an incident. Alert, decide, then go through the normal pipeline.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why parallel decoding breaks, and how to make it fast
md: Diffusion decoding uses fewer sequential passes but more total compute per answer. It wins wall-clock time only when each pass is memory-bound (small batches, interactive latency): lesson 1's estimate gives an H100 room for about 295 tokens per pass at the cost of one. Caching and confidence thresholds exist to shrink the compute overhead without giving back the parallelism.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Moving the KV cache: bytes, links and overlap
md: Overlap hides latency, not bandwidth. If two prefill GPUs share that 25 Gb/s link and each finishes an 8K prompt every 1.45 s, they produce about 1.4 caches/s against a link that sustains about 1.5. Add a third and the link becomes the bottleneck, however well transfers overlap.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Carving: recovering files with no metadata at all
md: A carved file has no name, no path, no timestamps and no owner. You can testify that these bytes were on the disk at this offset. Who created them, and when, needs other evidence.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Why a billion vectors break in-memory graph indexes
md: Two numbers drive an SSD-resident index: **total reads per query** (limits throughput, since the SSD has a fixed IOPS budget) and **round trips per query** (limits latency, since each trip costs a few hundred microseconds). DiskANN attacks both: a graph with short search paths, and a search that issues several reads per round trip.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: When preferences look certain: DPO overfits, IPO holds
md: Do not read DPO's $\beta$ as a guarantee of staying close to the reference. On pairs the model already separates, DPO's gradient shrinks but never pushes back, so drift continues as long as you keep training. The IPO paper notes that early stopping is the usual extra guard.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Backfilling history without overwriting newer writes
md: A backfill copy is always an *old* view of a row. Whatever mechanism you use (insert-if-absent, versions, or watermarks), it must guarantee that a backfilled row can never land after a newer write for the same key, and that deletes are remembered.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Probes: kprobes, tracepoints, fentry, uprobes and profile
md: Probe context matters. `tracepoint:block:block_rq_issue` often fires in the context of the process that issued the I/O, but it can also fire from kernel context (for example readahead, where the kernel reads file pages before anyone asks for them), so `comm` and `pid` may not name the application you expect.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Edge devices: the doors attackers now try first
md: A common misconception: "it is a security product, so it is secure". Firewalls and VPNs are software written under the same pressures as any other, and they run on the most exposed spot you have. KEV counts measure exploitation that was found and reported, which also depends on how widely a product is deployed; they are not a ranking of code quality.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: The patch race: KEV-driven deadlines for edge devices
md: Mitigation is not remediation, and patching is not the end. For a KEV edge bug that is automatable or gives total control, assume exploitation may have come first: patch within days, then look for signs it already happened.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Why RL makes reasoning long: the length bias in the policy loss
md: The two papers do not agree on the exact mechanism. Fatemi et al. argue that the $1/|o_i|$ account is incomplete, because a longer response also adds more terms to the sum being divided. They agree on the direction that matters in practice: negative advantages pull toward longer responses, positive ones toward shorter. The share of wrong answers in training therefore steers length.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Budget forcing, effort levels and hard caps at inference
md: Inference-time levers are cheap but blunt: forcing a stop interrupts reasoning, forcing 'Wait' saturates. Training-time methods (preference pairs, length rewards, LCPO) teach the model to plan a shorter trace, which is why L1 beats budget forcing at small budgets.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: HTML character references and the order a browser decodes
md: Decoding order is outside-in: HTML first, then URL, then script. Check the innermost value as plain data, then encode it for each outer layer on the way out.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: JSON differentials: duplicate keys, numbers and CouchDB
md: Reject duplicate keys and out-of-range numbers at the first parser, then pass the parsed (or re-serialised, canonical) object onward. Never forward the original bytes to a second parser and assume it reads them the same way.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Worked configs: SwiftOnSecurity's sysmon-config and sysmon-modular
md: A Sysmon config is a written decision about what you will be able to investigate later. Read what your config excludes as carefully as what it includes, and keep it in version control like detection rules (logging-detection-engineering).

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: One meter, many appliances: the disaggregation problem
md: Real aggregates are not the clean sum of the appliances you know about. UK-DALE reports that in House 1, with monitors on almost every appliance, only 80% of the energy was sub-metered, partly because the 52 plug monitors themselves draw about 50 W. The $\varepsilon_t$ term is never zero.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Cleaning: Unicode, case, punctuation and legal suffixes
md: Stripping is lossy. NFKC turns the superscript in `i⁹` into a plain `9`, and a stopword list (words deleted from every key because they seem uninformative) that drops `group`, `bank` or `the` can merge different companies. Strip only tokens that never distinguish entities in your data, apply cleaning to the matching key, and keep the original string.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: A tenant: the cloud directory behind every Microsoft 365 login
md: A tenant is a token issuer that many services trust. The questions that decide its security are: who can get a token, for which app, with which permissions, from where, and for how long.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Case: Midnight Blizzard inside Microsoft's own tenant (2024)
md: Midnight Blizzard turned one unprotected account into mailbox access through apps: find an app with power, create apps of your own, grant them an application permission. Defend by inventorying every tenant and app, enforcing MFA everywhere, and alerting on grants of high-risk application permissions.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Token theft and replay, and binding tokens to devices
md: Passkeys protect the login; device binding protects what the login produces. Use both, plus a compliant-device requirement, and keep revocation and CAE ready for the replay that gets through.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: The logs: sign-ins, audit, Graph activity and MailItemsAccessed
md: Sign-in logs say who got tokens, audit logs say what changed, Graph activity logs say what apps asked for, and MailItemsAccessed says which mail was touched. Export all four before you need them: default retention is 7 or 30 days.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: The winner's curse: why the best public score is too high
md: The maximum of many noisy scores is biased upward. Selecting a system on a query set uses up that set: its score for the winner is no longer an unbiased estimate. The bias grows with the number of systems tried (roughly like sqrt(ln N)) and shrinks with more queries (like 1/sqrt(n)).

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Contamination: when test queries leak into training data
md: Putting it together: split by query cluster and time, tune on dev, read a sealed and rotating test set rarely, report paired bootstrap CIs, correct for every comparison you run, and check for contamination with fresh queries the model could not have seen.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: What each mitigation does not stop, and where to practise
md: Combine layers so their blind spots do not line up: canary plus shadow stack or PAC for returns, CFI for forward edges, full RELRO for the GOT, PIE with high-entropy ASLR and no leaks, tagging or hardened allocators for the heap, and a sandbox around anything that parses untrusted input. Then keep fixing bugs.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: FedAvg exactly, worked on three clients over two rounds
md: A common misreading is that FedAvg averages the clients' answers. It averages their **parameters**. In this problem the sample-weighted average of the three local optima is 1.667 and the plain average is 2.0, while the true optimum is 2.3. Averaging models that have fully solved their own problems gives the wrong model.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-1: expand at search time instead of build time
md: ACORN-$\gamma$ and ACORN-1 run the same search strategy, predicate subgraph traversal. They differ only in *where* the denser neighborhood comes from: stored at build time (ACORN-$\gamma$, faster search, slower build) or reconstructed from two-hop lookups at query time (ACORN-1, cheap build, somewhat slower search).

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Online softmax: exact attention one block at a time
md: Online softmax is exact. The running max is only for numerical safety (keeping $e^x$ from overflowing); any consistent reference point gives the same $O/l$. Every FlashAttention version computes the same math; they differ only in how the work is mapped onto the hardware.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: The training target: straight lines and their velocity
md: The training loss does not go to zero even for a perfect network. Different pairs pass through the same $(x_t, t)$ with different targets, and a regression can only output their average. That average is the field you want, as lesson 3 shows.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Refinement: proving a detailed design implements an abstract one
md: Implementation is implication: the detailed spec, seen through a refinement mapping, must allow only behaviors the abstract spec allows. Extra internal steps are fine because they map to stuttering steps.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: What 8 and 4 bits can hold: E4M3, E5M2 and E2M1
md: Exponent bits buy **range**, mantissa bits buy **precision**. E4M3 rounds with at most 6.25% relative error but spans only about 18 binades; E5M2 spans about 32 binades at 12.5%; E2M1 (FP4) spans 3.58 binades at up to 25%.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: NVFP4: 16-value blocks, E4M3 scales and a tensor scale
md: In NVFP4 the amax of every 16-value block is encoded at close to FP8 precision (the block scale is E4M3), which is at least 1/16 = 6.25% of all values. MXFP4 stores every value, the amax included, at FP4 precision behind a power-of-two scale.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Network and device signals: IPs, proxies and fingerprints
md: Never trust a device signal you did not verify. A header or a JavaScript value is a claim made by the client. Use it to raise suspicion when claims disagree or repeat across many accounts, not to grant trust on its own.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Promotion and referral abuse: multi-accounting and holds
md: Every promotion is a price per account. Tie it to a scarce identity, check the link between referrer and referee, and hold the payout until the qualifying payment can no longer be reversed.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: From risk score to decision: rules, models, step-up and review
md: Pick actions by expected cost: allow when $pL$ is small, block when $(1-p)G$ is small, and step up in between when the challenge catches more fraud than it costs in lost customers.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Why write() returning does not mean your data is safe
md: Calling fsync on a file does not necessarily make the file's **directory entry** durable. A newly created or renamed file also needs an fsync on a file descriptor for the directory, or after a crash the name may be missing.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: A real hunt with libFuzzer: harness, run log and the crash
md: A harness plus a sanitizer turns 'run the parser on generated bytes' into an automatic bug finder: coverage guidance reaches deep code, comparison tracing gets past magic values, and ASan converts silent corruption into a report with a saved reproducer.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Protocol and stateful fuzzing, and the Broadcom Wi-Fi case
md: Stateful targets need stateful fuzzing: keep a valid prefix, mutate later messages, use responses or coverage to recognise new states, and reset the target between sequences. Firmware that skips basic mitigations (no stack cookies) makes every such bug worse.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Filling the Wagner-Fischer table cell by cell
md: The table gives one number, but several different edit sequences can tie for the minimum. The traceback picks one of them. Do not read a single alignment as *the* explanation of how two strings differ.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
md: Invariant does not mean mirror-proof. Some cameras and optical paths flip the image. Astrometry.net's code-flip helper swaps each (x, y) pair, and the solver defaults to trying both parities (parity here means whether the image is mirrored or not). Groth's triangle method instead records whether vertices run clockwise and accepts either sense.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Radius search: cover with cells, then check exact distance
md: `WHERE ST_Distance(a, b) < 500` gives the right answer but cannot use the spatial index, so it scans every row. The PostGIS docs pair them deliberately: use `ST_DWithin` to limit the search with the index, then `ST_Distance` only for sorting the few survivors.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
md: Misconception: "nvidia-smi shows 20 GB used, so my tensors use 20 GB." It shows reserved memory plus the CUDA context: the driver's per-process state on the GPU, such as loaded kernel code and the driver's own buffers, which uses device memory that PyTorch's counters never include. Compare `memory_allocated()` with `memory_reserved()` before hunting for a leak.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: From registers to HBM: the GPU memory map
md: **Local memory is not local to the chip.** The word refers to scope (one thread), not location. Spilled registers, large per-thread arrays and arrays indexed with values the compiler cannot resolve at compile time all go to local memory, which has the latency and bandwidth of global memory.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Case study: one matrix transpose, three kernels
md: The NVIDIA post's conclusion: coalescing global memory accesses is by far the most critical step. Use shared memory to turn strided global access into coalesced access, then check the shared access for bank conflicts.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: How profiling perturbs what it measures
md: Decide which question you are asking before you choose the flags. Isolated-kernel analysis wants the defaults: locked clocks, flushed caches, serialized launches. System-representative behavior wants `--replay-mode application --clock-control none --cache-control none`. Mixing the two across runs produces numbers that disagree for reasons that have nothing to do with your code.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: From chunks to an entity graph with LLM extraction
md: The graph is an LLM's *abstractive summary* of the corpus (written in the model's own words, not copied sentences), not a parse of it. Every node and edge carries an LLM-written description, and those descriptions, not the raw text, are what later stages summarize.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: RLVR: replacing the reward model with a program
md: Verifiable does not mean perfect. A verifier can reject correct answers (12.0 versus 12) or accept wrong ones (a unit-test suite that misses edge cases). Real pipelines normalize answers; for example, Tulu 3's 'flex' MATH evaluation tries three different ways to extract the final answer, because models often ignore the requested format. The quality of the checker caps the quality of the signal.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: What a GTFS Schedule zip contains and how its tables join
md: A stop can appear twice in one trip, for example on a loop route where the bus starts and ends at the same stop. That is why `stop_sequence`, not `stop_id`, identifies a row of a trip. Code that keys stop times by `stop_id` alone silently overwrites one visit with the other.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Phone phreaking: when the voice line was also the control line
md: Filtering out the 2600 Hz tone would have been a weak fix: phreaks used many other tones, and a filter on a shared channel is always a race. Removing the attacker's access to the control channel ended the whole class of trick.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Conficker: the botnet that made the industry organise
md: Conficker showed both sides of collective defence: an industry coalition could deny a botnet its control channel at internet scale, but cleaning millions of unmanaged PCs was beyond it. Patching (MS08-067 was a month old) and removing risky defaults (AutoRun) would have prevented most infections.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: SolarWinds and Log4Shell: what you install and what you import
md: SolarWinds attacked what you install (a trusted vendor's build), Log4Shell lived in what you import (a free library inside other products). The responses were inventory (SBOMs), verifiable builds, least privilege for powerful tools like network monitors, and review boards that turn incidents into public lessons.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: What a side channel is: secrets leaking through how code runs
md: A side-channel attack does not break the mathematics. It breaks the assumption that an implementation reveals only its outputs. Every defence in this course makes some byproduct independent of the secret, hides the secret from the computation that leaks, or keeps the observer away.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: One request, two readers: why proxies and caches disagree
md: Testing a site's proxies or cache for these bugs can harm *other* users, because the leftover bytes or poisoned entries land on real people. Test only systems you own or have written permission to test, and prefer your own lab: the toys in this course run entirely in one Python process.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: How HTTP caches decide: keys, freshness and Vary
md: A cache key is a promise: "any two requests with this key deserve the same response". Every attack in the next lessons breaks that promise, either because the response depended on something outside the key, or because two different resources ended up under one key.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: hugetlbfs: a reserved pool you map on purpose
md: A pool is memory you have given away. Those 3170 pages hold 6.2 GiB out of the page cache (the kernel's in-memory cache of file data) and away from every other process whether or not PostgreSQL is running. Over-sizing `nr_hugepages` is a common way to cause out-of-memory kills on a box that looks half empty.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Counting cache bytes: growing KV cache plus a fixed state
md: Hybrids do not help much at short context. At 1,024 tokens the cache formula gives only about 1.9x less memory for Nemotron-H-8B, and both the Jamba and NVIDIA papers report similar speed to Transformers at small context lengths. The gains grow with context and batch size.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Why a raw query is a poor probe for an unsupervised encoder
md: Short queries and long documents look different. A label-free encoder knows what *documents* resemble each other, but nobody taught it what *answers a question*. HyDE's trick is to stop comparing a question with answers at all.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Zones and conduits: the ISA/IEC 62443 way to segment
md: Zones are not VLANs. A VLAN (virtual LAN) is one way to separate traffic, but NIST lists VLANs as logical separation 'when physical separation may not be feasible'. A zone boundary needs an enforcement point, and a misconfigured switch trunk can quietly merge two zones.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Segmentation, DMZs, one-way gateways and allowlisting
md: A firewall rule that says 'allow 10.0.0.0/8 to OT, any port, temporary' is the most common way segmentation fails. Review the rule table regularly, expire temporary rules automatically, and alert on hits to rule 11: traffic nobody planned is either a misconfiguration or an intruder.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Inside a SAML response: Issuer, Subject, Conditions and statements
md: Attributes are authorization input. An SP that maps `groups=admins` in the assertion to admin rights hands role decisions to whoever controls assertion content: the IdP's administrators, anyone who compromises them, and anyone who can get an unsigned assertion past the SP.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Conditional access: deciding at sign-in, and what happens after
md: Conditional access decides at the moment of issuance. Everything after that moment is protected by token lifetime, session binding and signals, so a policy is only as strong as the session it produces.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Leavers: deprovisioning, SCIM and the Cash App download
md: Disabling the IdP account is not deprovisioning. It blocks the next single sign-on. Sessions already open, tokens already issued, local accounts and shared passwords all survive it.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Measuring identity hygiene, detecting abuse, and running the programme
md: Measure the tail, not just the median: one leaver with 400 hours of access matters more than a good average. Pair hygiene metrics (orphans, dormant, standing privilege, owners) with detections for terminated logins, out-of-process grants, vault and break-glass use.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Events, alerts and incidents: when does it become an incident?
md: An incident starts when the attacker acts, not when you declare it. The HSE intrusion began on 18 March 2021 and was declared on 14 May. The gap (dwell time) is what your logs, memory and timeline work must reach back across.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Acquisition: memory, disk images, cloud snapshots and logs
md: Encryption changes the plan. If a disk uses BitLocker or another full-disk encryption, an image taken after power-off is unreadable without the recovery key. Capture what you need from the running system, or make sure the key is in your hands before you shut it down.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Blameless postmortems, lessons learned and tabletop exercises
md: Blameless does not mean nobody is accountable. It means the review asks why the system let a reasonable person make that choice, and fixes the system: alert routing, ownership, tooling, training.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Why epoll plus read still costs a syscall per I/O
md: epoll is a **readiness** API: it tells you when an operation *could* succeed, then you do it. io_uring is a **completion** API: you describe the operation (read these bytes into this buffer), and the kernel tells you when it is *done* and what it returned.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Threat modelling a device: who can reach it, and how
md: A common mistake is to skip the physical position because "attackers would need the device". Attackers can buy the device. The right question is what one opened unit gives them: its owner's data (acceptable for many products) or a key to all units (never acceptable).

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Medical devices: FDA section 524B, pacemakers and insulin pumps
md: A medical maker cannot ship fixes as casually as a phone maker: each change may need risk review, and an implant update happens in a clinic. That is why FDA expects the update path and the postmarket plan to be designed before approval, not invented after a disclosure.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Fixing ReDoS: rewrite, bound, change engines, cap the input
md: Both V8 modes are experimental, and the blog says the fallback skips patterns with backreferences, lookarounds, large bounded repeats, or the `u` and `i` flags. Treat the flag as a safety net that you test with your own patterns, not as the fix. Rewriting and bounding input are the fixes.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: One skeleton, three allocators: size classes and caches
md: Every production allocator is the same four layers: size classes, a lock-free local cache, a shared per-size-class middle, and a page-level back-end that talks to the OS. The interesting differences are *who owns the local cache* (thread, CPU, or page), *how objects freed by another thread get home*, and *when idle pages go back to the OS*.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Elle: catching isolation anomalies in transactions
md: Elle never solves for a transaction order. It designs the workload so reads expose the version order, then turns the history into a dependency graph and looks for cycles. A cycle is a concrete, explainable counterexample, and its edge types name the anomaly.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The per-packet budget: why the kernel path runs out of cycles
md: Kernel bypass means the **device driver lives in your process**. Data moves between device and application memory by DMA, the application learns about it by polling memory, and nothing on the per-packet or per-I/O path enters the kernel.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Why chains of elementwise ops are memory bound
md: Misconception: "the GPU is slow at GELU because tanh is expensive". Profile first. A standalone GELU kernel on a large tensor is limited by the read and the write of the tensor, not by tanh.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: A patient and consistent teacher: the recipe that makes KD work
md: Caching teacher outputs is only safe when the student's input is exactly the cached input. With random crops, flips, noise or mixup on the student side, cache the augmentation too or run the teacher live on the same batch. For language models the input is the token sequence itself, so the same rule says: teacher and student must score the same tokens.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs
md: Distillation trades extra training compute (running a teacher) for a cheaper model to serve. It works best when the student can realistically imitate the teacher; when the gap is large, shrink it with an assistant or an easier teacher.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Beyond rounding: pre-RoPE keys, outliers, and FP8 in production
md: FP8 without calibration uses a scale of 1.0. That works when values fit FP8's range, but calibrated scales are what vLLM recommends for best accuracy, and some layers (such as sliding-window ones, which attend only to a fixed number of recent tokens) can be kept in the native dtype, the model's own number format.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Hiding the transfer: layer-wise loading and asynchronous saving
md: Overlap turns load plus compute into roughly max(load, compute). It is free speed when the two are balanced and nearly useless when one dominates.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Vector clocks: detecting concurrency exactly
md: Lamport clocks give one-way causality in one integer. Vector clocks give exact causality and detect concurrency, at the cost of one integer per node in every timestamp and every message.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: ColPali: late interaction over page images
md: Late interaction is not free accuracy. You pay in index size, in memory bandwidth at query time, and in engine support. For large text corpora a common design is a cheap first stage (BM25 or a single-vector index) with ColBERT or ColPali scoring a few hundred candidates.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Latent search: one thought, several frontier nodes
md: BFS-like (breadth-first-search-like) is an interpretation from probing, not a built-in algorithm. Coconut was never trained to search, keeps no explicit visited set, and the parallelism narrows after a couple of thoughts.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: An index is a model: predicting where a key sits
md: A learned index does not return approximate answers. It finds exactly the same record a B-tree would. Only the *path* to the record is approximate; the final local search makes the answer exact.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: From MLM logits to one weight per vocabulary term
md: Misconception: the expansion terms are synonyms. They are whatever the MLM head plus ranking training found useful. The paper's own example document about bow legs gains *leg* and *treatment*, but also *arrow* (bow and arrow) and *teeth*, with small weights.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaMART in practice: libraries, truncation and click bias
md: In production, LambdaMART is the training objective of a tree ensemble that rescores the top candidates of a first-stage retriever. Its quality depends on labels (judgments or debiased clicks), query-grouped data, and a truncation level that matches the positions users see.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: One family, many transitions: RetNet to GLA, Mamba2, RWKV-7, KDA
md: To place a new linear-attention layer, ask two questions. What is $A_t$: identity, scalar, diagonal, identity minus rank 1, or diagonal plus low rank? And what does the write minimize: a dot-product reward (additive) or a regression error (delta)? Richer $A_t$ means finer forgetting and a costlier kernel.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Processes, PIDs, process trees and signals
md: Read processes as a tree. Who started a process (its parent, its user, its command line in `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`) usually tells you more than its name, because names are trivial to fake.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: What an intruder touches: persistence and where defenders look
md: Do not investigate a live compromise only with the compromised system's own tools if you can avoid it: an intruder with root can alter `ps`, `ls` or the logs. Cross-check with package verification, a trusted copy of the tools, or off-host data.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring a service sandbox with systemd-analyze security
md: `systemd-analyze security` turns sandboxing into a number you can track per unit and gate in CI with `--offline=yes --threshold=`. Lower is better, but the score covers only systemd's own settings and cannot tell you what the service legitimately needs.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Falco: turning the system call stream into alerts
md: Falco = driver (modern eBPF by default) + state + YAML rules (condition, output, priority, macros, lists). It detects, it does not block. Every exclusion you add is a deliberate blind spot; write it down.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Patching a fleet: automatic updates, restarts, reboots and rings
md: Automate installation (unattended-upgrades, dnf-automatic), automate restarts (needrestart), schedule reboots or livepatch urgent kernel fixes, roll out in rings with canaries, and verify the running version, not the package database.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Judge biases: position, verbosity and self-preference
md: For pointwise relevance grades the order bias has an analogue: grading many passages in one prompt lets earlier passages anchor later ones. Grade one passage per call, as the Bing and UMBRELA prompts do, or randomise and repeat if you batch.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Threat model: how an LLM app gets attacked or goes wrong
md: OWASP's top LLM risk guidance says it is unclear whether fool-proof prevention of prompt injection exists, and recommends treating the model as an untrusted user. Design so that a fully hijacked model still cannot do much damage: least-privilege tools (each tool gets only the permissions its job needs), human approval for high-risk actions, and checks outside the model.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Fragmentation, and block tables as page tables
md: Paging does not shrink the KV cache. A 1,500-token sequence still needs 1,500 tokens of K and V. Paging removes the memory that held *nothing*, which is why the gain is largest when requests are short relative to their maximum length.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Constrained decoding: masking logits with a state machine
md: Constrained decoding does not make the model understand the format. It removes the illegal choices at each step and lets the model choose among what is left. An FSM state tells you which tokens are legal; a precomputed index makes that lookup cheap.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Evaluating the parser with exact match per field
md: Errors are not equal. A **spurious** filter (q6's remote_ok, q7's required javascript) removes good results and the user never sees them. A **missing** filter only returns extra results the user can see and skip. Track precision and recall of slots separately and weight spurious filters as the worse error.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Distilled 7B rerankers versus a cross-encoder: choosing a design
md: Write the cost model before choosing the method: calls on the critical path, input tokens, output tokens, and model size. Then check quality on your own queries: the cheapest design that holds your NDCG@10 wins.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Managed routing in Amazon Bedrock, and how routers fail
md: Routing failures are silent. A wrong answer from the weak model looks like any other answer, and the dashboard shows only that costs went down. Log the routed model with every response (Bedrock returns it), and compare quality by route, not just overall.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: RANSAC: keeping only matches that agree on one homography
md: A homography is only correct for planar scenes or pure camera rotation. For a general 3D scene seen from two positions, matches satisfy a fundamental or essential matrix instead, and forcing a homography will reject many correct matches.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Freeing nodes safely: hazard pointers and epochs
md: EBR is fast because readers only write their own epoch when they pin, but it is not strictly lock-free for memory: Fraser notes that a process that stalls inside a critical region stops the limbo lists (Fraser's name for the per-epoch garbage bags) from ever being reclaimed. Hazard pointers bound the unreclaimed memory (at most NR nodes) at the cost of publishing and re-validating every pointer before use.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drift when a release changes the format, and a pipeline that holds
md: The whole course in one line: a log template is the cheapest useful abstraction over log text, and the only one that turns an unbounded stream of unique strings into a small set of countable events. Everything after it, counting, baselining, sequence models, dashboards, inherits both its power and its errors.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Sigma: one rule format, many SIEMs
md: A converted query is only as right as its pipeline's field mapping. If your SIEM stores Sysmon in a different source, or the 4688 field is NewProcessName rather than Image, the query is valid, runs, and silently matches nothing. Always test converted rules against real events from your own environment.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Position Interpolation and NTK-aware scaling
md: Uniform interpolation protects the slow pairs but blurs the fast ones. Every better method since PI is about treating pairs differently according to their wavelength.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Depth without parameters: what looping a block buys
md: Looping saves **parameters** (memory, communication), not **compute**. Every loop is another full pass through the block, and the passes are sequential, so a $(1 \otimes 12)$ model is about as slow per token as a 12-layer model. Looped models trade memory for depth, they do not make inference free.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Build it: loop your GPT with input injection and random depth
md: Turning a GPT into a recurrent-depth model takes a split into prelude, core and coda, a concat adapter, a noise start and a random-depth training loop. The monitor that matters is the gap between low-r and high-r validation loss.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Counting parameters, choosing targets, merging for free inference
md: Merging has a price: a merged model serves one adapter. Hu et al. note it is not straightforward to batch requests for *different* adapters in one forward pass once A and B are folded into W. Serving many adapters at once needs the unmerged form, which is the subject of the multi-LoRA serving course.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Unlearning by replacement: Who's Harry Potter and RMU
md: Replacement methods give the model something specific to do instead: predict generic tokens (WHP) or produce scrambled activations on hazardous inputs (RMU). That avoids gradient ascent's collapse, but the target behavior is defined only on the inputs you trained on.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: How a Mac defends itself: the layers from boot to app
md: Each macOS control answers one question. When you investigate a Mac incident, ask which question the attacker never had to face: was the code never quarantined, was it signed and notarized, did the user approve a prompt, did it run as a script rather than an app?

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Endpoint Security: the API every Mac EDR is built on
md: Endpoint Security is to a Mac what kernel callbacks plus ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) are to Windows: the one place a security product can see every exec, file open, login and permission change, and block some of them. When choosing a Mac EDR, ask which ES events it subscribes to and which it uses in AUTH mode.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: The malware economy: loaders, access brokers and RaaS
md: Ransomware is the last step of a chain, not the first. Loader infections, sold remote-access logins and hands-on intrusion usually come days or weeks before encryption, which is your window to detect and evict.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Command and control: beacons, jitter and Cobalt Strike
md: Regular is not the same as malicious. Software updaters, mail clients, telemetry and monitoring agents all beacon. Use regularity to rank what to review, then check the destination (age of domain, reputation, who else talks to it) and the process that made the connections (Sysmon event 3).

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Truncate, then re-normalize: the mechanics on a toy vector
md: Re-normalizing the query alone never changes a ranking: it scales every score by the same number. What changes rankings is the documents' prefix lengths, so re-normalize the stored document prefixes (or compute true cosine). OpenAI's embedding guide says the same: if you shorten vectors yourself, normalize them.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP
md: The 5as/h term assumes attention materializes the s x s score matrix. Fused attention kernels (FlashAttention, Dao et al. 2022, which computes attention tile by tile in fast on-chip memory; also in NVIDIA's Transformer Engine library) never store it, so most of that term disappears by itself. Megatron Core's config even warns that with fused attention there is no need to put core_attn in --recompute-modules.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Hands on: plan, launch, profile and checkpoint an MCore run
md: Plan with the formulas (state, activations, bubble), launch with flags that encode the plan, measure MFU against a named peak, profile for exposed communication and bubbles, and checkpoint in a format you can reshard.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Handles, mutexes, sockets and registry hives in memory
md: Every network row in memory names its owning process, and every handle names its holder. That pairing (this PID talked to that address, this PID opened that process) is what turns a list of artefacts into an attribution inside the host.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Size classes: buying speed with internal waste
md: `sizeof` is not what you pay. With a million 130-byte records you might budget 124 MiB, but jemalloc hands out 160 bytes each (153 MiB) and a power-of-two allocator 256 (244 MiB). Measure with `malloc_usable_size` or allocator stats, not by multiplying `sizeof`.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Acquire and release: publishing data across threads
md: Synchronization needs a pair on the same atomic: a Release (or stronger) write and an Acquire (or stronger) read that observes that write or its release sequence. Then everything before the write is visible after the read.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: RCU: publish a new version, free the old after a grace period
md: RCU protects readers from updaters, not updaters from each other. `rcu_assign_pointer()` does not make two concurrent updates safe; the example still takes `foo_mutex`. And a pointer from `rcu_dereference()` is valid only inside the critical section that fetched it.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Heap overflow: corrupting the neighbouring object
